title: Intermediate, Posterior, Pan-uveitis and Miscellaneous Disorders

questions.q: Intermediate uveitis is also known as ___.
questions.exp: Intermediate Uveitis: Also known as pars planitis. (Book p191)

questions.q: What is the most common cause of intermediate uveitis?
questions.exp: Causes: 1. Idiopathic (m/c); 2. Associated with Lyme's disease, sarcoidosis, multiple sclerosis, tuberculosis. (Book p191)

questions.q: Intermediate uveitis is associated with all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Associated with: Lyme's disease, sarcoidosis, multiple sclerosis, tuberculosis. (VKH syndrome is listed under pan-uveitis.) (Book p191)

questions.q: A patient reports bilateral floaters and blurring of vision. Which uveitis does the book describe with these symptoms?
questions.exp: Intermediate uveitis symptoms: B/L floaters; blurring of vision. (Book p191)

questions.q: In intermediate uveitis, the anterior segment shows ___ anterior uveitis.
questions.exp: Signs: Spillover anterior uveitis. (Book p191)

questions.q: In intermediate uveitis, 'snowballs' are:
opts: Aggregations of cells in the vitreous
questions.exp: Snowballs: Aggregation of cells in vitreous. (Book p191)

questions.q: In intermediate uveitis, what is the first step of steroid treatment, and what is the next step if it fails?
opts: Systemic steroids; then posterior subtenon injection
Posterior subtenon steroid injection; then systemic steroids
Systemic steroids; then pars plana vitrectomy
questions.exp: Treatment: Steroids: posterior subtenon injection; if fails -> steroids: systemic. (Book p191)

questions.q: Intermediate uveitis has failed posterior subtenon and systemic steroids. Which immunomodulatory drug is next?
questions.exp: If fails -> immunomodulatory drugs: azathioprine. (Book p191)

questions.q: If azathioprine also fails in intermediate uveitis, the book advises:
opts: Pars plana vitrectomy plus photocoagulation of the snowbank
questions.exp: If fails -> Pars plana vitrectomy + Photocoagulation of snowbank. (Book p191)

questions.q: Snowbanking in intermediate uveitis is a:
opts: Aggregation of cells in the vitreous
questions.exp: Snowbanking: Fibrovascular plaque. (Book p191)

questions.q: Which condition is the most common cause of vision loss in intermediate uveitis?
questions.exp: Cystoid macular edema: m/c cause of vision loss. (Book p191)

questions.q: Posterior uveitis (chorioretinitis) is inflammation of the choroid and ___.
questions.exp: Posterior Uveitis/Chorioretinitis: Inflammation of choroid & retina. (Book p191)

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT among the listed clinical features of posterior uveitis?
questions.exp: Clinical features: 1. Floaters 2. Painless loss of vision 3. Scotoma 4. Metamorphopsia 5. Photopsia. (Book p191)

questions.q: Metamorphopsia is distortion of image. Which feature is listed fifth after it?
questions.exp: 4. Metamorphopsia: Distortion of image. 5. Photopsia. (Book p191)

questions.q: What is the most common infectious cause of posterior uveitis in the table?
questions.exp: Infectious: 1. Most common: Toxoplasmosis. (Book p192)

questions.q: Match the stage of toxoplasmosis with its fundus appearance — 1) Active  2) Chronic  … A) Punched out scar  B) Headlight in fog appearance  C) Candle wax dripping appearance
questions.exp: Active: headlight in fog appearance (d/t associated active vitritis). Chronic: punched out scar. (Book p192)

questions.q: Cats are the definitive hosts for the organism that causes focal chorioretinitis. Which infection?
questions.exp: Cats are definitive hosts. Toxoplasmosis causes focal chorioretinitis. (Book p192)

questions.q: A child has unilateral loss of vision with leukocoria (white pupillary reflex). Which infectious cause does the table list?
questions.exp: 2. Toxocariasis: Unilateral LOV; Leukocoria (white pupillary reflex). (Book p192)

questions.q: Which infection is the most common cause of loss of vision in ocular HIV?
questions.exp: 3. CMV retinitis: m/c cause of LOV in ocular HIV. (Book p192)

questions.q: Which appearance is NOT described for CMV retinitis?
questions.exp: CMV retinitis: a. Pizza pie appearance; b. Scrambled egg & ketchup appearance; c. Brushfire extension. (Candle wax dripping is sarcoidosis.) (Book p192)

questions.q: Besides toxoplasmosis, toxocariasis and CMV retinitis, which is listed as an infectious cause?
questions.exp: Infectious: 1. Toxoplasmosis 2. Toxocariasis 3. CMV retinitis 4. TB. Sarcoidosis, Behcet's and birdshot are non-infectious. (Book p192)

questions.q: A fundus shows a candle wax dripping appearance. What is the cause of this appearance in sarcoidosis?
questions.exp: Sarcoidosis: candle wax dripping appearance (d/t perivascular inflammation & sheathing). (Book p192)

questions.q: In sarcoidosis, Lander's sign refers to ___.
questions.exp: Lander's sign: Pre-retinal nodules. (Book p192)

questions.q: Which of the following is listed under NON-infectious causes of posterior uveitis?
questions.exp: Non-infectious: 1. Sarcoidosis 2. Behcet's disease 3. Birdshot chorioretinopathy 4. Serpiginous choroiditis. (Book p192)

questions.q: Match the condition with its HLA association — 1) Birdshot chorioretinopathy  2) Serpiginous choroiditis  … A) HLA B7  B) HLA A29  C) HLA B27
questions.exp: Birdshot chorioretinopathy: HLA A29 association. Serpiginous choroiditis: HLA B7 association. (Book p192)

questions.q: Match the pattern with its causes — 1) Focal chorioretinitis  2) Multifocal chorioretinitis  … A) Toxoplasma, Toxocariasis, CMV  B) HSV, TB, syphilis  C) Toxoplasma, TB, syphilis
questions.exp: Focal chorioretinitis: Toxoplasma, Toxocariasis, CMV. Multifocal chorioretinitis: HSV, TB, syphilis. (Book p192)

questions.q: Treatment of infectious posterior uveitis is:
opts: Treat the cause plus systemic steroids
questions.exp: Treatment: 1. Infectious cases: Treat the cause + systemic steroids. (Book p193)

questions.q: For non-infectious posterior uveitis (alternative to systemic steroids), match the drug with its study — 1) Adalimumab  2) Sirolimus  3) Voclosporin  … A) Luminate trials  B) Visual studies I to II  C) Sakura program
questions.exp: Non-infectious cases: systemic steroids OR adalimumab (visual studies I to II); sirolimus (Sakura program); voclosporin (Luminate trials). (Book p193)

questions.q: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) syndrome affects which four structures?
opts: Eye, skin, meninges and parotid gland
questions.exp: VKH syndrome affects: Eye, Ears, Skin, Meninges. (Book p193)

questions.q: The ocular involvement in VKH is bilateral ___ panuveitis.
questions.exp: Eye: B/L granulomatous panuveitis. (Book p193)

questions.q: 'Sunset glow fundus' in VKH results from:
questions.exp: Sunset glow fundus: RPE atrophy. (Book p193)

questions.q: A VKH patient shows perilimbal vitiligo. What is this sign called?
questions.exp: Suiguira sign: Perilimbal vitiligo. (Book p193)

questions.q: Which type of retinal detachment is listed in the eye findings of VKH?
opts: Total RD from a giant tear
questions.exp: VKH eye: Exudative RD. (Book p193)

questions.q: Match the VKH structure with its finding — 1) Ears  2) Skin  3) Meninges  … A) Vitiligo  B) Meningoencephalitis  C) Tinnitus
questions.exp: Ears: tinnitus; skin: vitiligo; meninges: meningoencephalitis. (Book p193)

questions.q: A patient develops granulomatous panuveitis after accidental penetrating trauma affecting the ciliary body. Which condition?
questions.exp: Sympathetic ophthalmitis: clinical feature granulomatous panuveitis; cause: accidental penetrating trauma affecting ciliary body. (Book p193)

questions.q: After trauma to one eye (exciting eye), sympathetic ophthalmitis appears in the other (sympathizing) eye after more than:
questions.exp: Pathogenesis: trauma to one eye (exciting eye) -> >2 weeks -> sympathetic ophthalmitis in other eye (sympathizing eye). (Book p193)

questions.q: To prevent sympathetic ophthalmitis, the traumatic eye should undergo enucleation within:
questions.exp: Prevention: Enucleation of traumatic eye in 14 days. (Book p193)

questions.q: Once sympathetic ophthalmitis has developed, the treatment given in the book is:
questions.exp: Treatment: Steroids. (Book p193)

questions.q: Match the procedure with its terminology — 1) Enucleation  2) Evisceration  3) Exenteration  … A) Removal of eye and orbital contents  B) Removal of whole eyeball + optic nerve  C) Removal of all layers of eyeball except sclera
questions.exp: Enucleation: removal of whole eyeball + optic nerve. Evisceration: removal of all layers of eyeball except sclera. Exenteration: removal of eye and orbital contents. (Book p194)

questions.q: Which indications does the table list for enucleation?
questions.exp: Indications - enucleation: retinoblastoma; trauma. (Book p194)

questions.q: Evisceration is indicated in:
questions.exp: Indications - evisceration: endophthalmitis. (Book p194)

questions.q: Exenteration is indicated in orbital mucormycosis and in:
questions.exp: Indications - exenteration: orbital mucormycosis; tumors metastasised to orbit. (Book p194)

questions.q: True or false — 'The table lists retinoblastoma as a contraindication for enucleation.' Choose the correct verdict:
opts: True - enucleation and evisceration are both contraindicated in retinoblastoma
False - retinoblastoma is a contraindication for exenteration
False - enucleation is contraindicated in panophthalmitis; retinoblastoma is the contraindication for evisceration
True - enucleation is contraindicated in retinoblastoma and panophthalmitis
questions.exp: C/I - enucleation: panophthalmitis; evisceration: retinoblastoma; exenteration: dash (-). (Book p194)

questions.q: The Appearance row of the table shows photographs of:
opts: Enucleation, evisceration and exenteration together with orbital mucormycosis
questions.exp: Appearance row: photographs under Enucleation, Evisceration and Exenteration. (Book p194)

questions.q: Gyrate atrophy is a type of ___ atrophy.
questions.exp: Gyrate atrophy: Type of choroid atrophy. (Book p194)

questions.q: What is the inheritance pattern of gyrate atrophy?
questions.exp: Gyrate atrophy: Autosomal recessive. (Book p194)

questions.q: Gyrate atrophy results from mutation in which gene, and what happens to ornithine?
opts: Ornithine aminotransferase gene; ornithine levels rise
Ornithine aminotransferase gene; ornithine levels fall
Arginine synthetase gene; ornithine levels fall
questions.exp: Mutation in ornithine aminotransferase gene: increased levels of ornithine. (Book p194)

questions.q: Treatment of gyrate atrophy is restriction of which dietary component, since ornithine is synthesised from it?
questions.exp: Treatment: Arginine restriction in diet (ornithine is synthesised from arginine). (Book p194)
